case.label: C
case.text: A reader could think failed processing leads to a dead-letter queue, but the stem says the queue uses default settings, which have no redrive policy, so nothing moves the message; it simply becomes visible again.

case.label: E
case.text: One FIFO queue per customer also gives per-customer order, exactly-once processing and parallelism across customers, so it meets the functional needs; only the LEAST operational overhead wording rules it out.

case.label: B
case.text: An SNS topic with filter policies on the message body also routes by fields and needs no routing code; it loses only because AWS service events and SaaS partner events cannot be sent to it natively.

case.label: A
case.text: A scheduled Lambda copy to S3 every day would keep every failed message beyond 10 days and is a plausible working design; only the overhead criterion makes it worse than a one-setting change.

case.label: C
case.text: Archiving every event through Firehose to S3 and republishing them keeps events for 30 days and permits reprocessing, so it works; it loses only on the amount of custom tooling versus a native archive and replay.

answers.flag: Option B says 'the new queue', which only exists in option E, so the options depend on each other; and option D (long retries) could be defended as surviving an outage of several hours if the delivery policy allows 24 hours.

case.label: D
case.text: A delivery policy that keeps retrying for 24 hours would cover an outage of several hours and needs no new resource, so a candidate could argue it prevents the loss; it does not keep an undelivered event for later resending, which the stem states.

case.label: D
case.text: A delay queue looks like the simplest way to hold a message for 3 days, but the SQS delay maximum is only 15 minutes, so it cannot hold the message that long (a candidate who forgets the limit would pick it).

case.label: D
case.text: SNS fan-out to one queue per service also buffers orders and survives an offline consumer, and it would allow later consumers; it is more than the single-consumer requirement needs.

case.label: A
case.text: A single queue decouples the order service from the others, but each message goes to only one consumer, so the three services would not each receive every event.

case.label: D
case.text: An EventBridge bus with a rule per service plus an SNS target for the SMS fan-out would also work, since all events are in-house; it adds a second service next to SNS, which is why it has more overhead.

case.label: C
case.text: Calling ChangeMessageVisibility from the workers also stops duplicate processing and can adapt to varying processing times; it needs code changes, so it loses on overhead.

case.label: B
case.text: FIFO with content-based deduplication removes duplicate sends and duplicate receives, so a candidate may think it fixes both causes; its deduplication interval is only 5 minutes, so a resend hours later still gets through.

case.label: B
case.text: A CloudTrail trail with S3 notifications would catch stop calls from the console, scripts and jobs, but log delivery is delayed and it needs custom parsing code, so it is worse on overhead and latency.

case.label: D
case.text: The visible-message count reflects the backlog, so a candidate may use it alone as a scaling signal; a fixed total ignores the instance count, so it does not scale in proportion.

case.label: D
case.text: One topic per order type routes the returns without a function and with no filtering; it needs every publisher changed, so it costs more development effort.

answers.flag: Option B (batch size 1) also retries only the malformed message and needs no code change, so with 'most operationally efficient' unspecified (code change versus invocation count) a careful candidate could defend B.

case.label: B
case.text: A batch size of 1 isolates every message, so only the malformed one fails and retries, and it needs only a configuration change with no code change; it costs more invocations and gives up batching, which the stem never says matters.

case.label: C
case.text: The stem does not say whether the subscription is confirmed, so a candidate could claim an unconfirmed subscription is the cause; the access policy that the queue was created with is the stated cause.

case.label: D
case.text: Moving the permission wholly to the queue policy looks like least privilege, but across accounts the caller's identity policy must also allow the action, so removing it from the role causes a denial.

case.label: B
case.text: A customer managed key in a CloudHSM-backed custom key store, with its key policy, also meets the rule that the company controls the key policy and could pair with the SNS key policy statement; it adds a CloudHSM cluster, so it loses on overhead.

case.label: B
case.text: Counting receives in the workers and moving a repeatedly failing message to another queue does the same job as a dead-letter queue; it needs custom code, so it has more overhead.

case.label: A
case.text: SNS to the HTTPS endpoints of the three services sends every order to every service with no queues to manage, and a candidate may assume retries cover short outages; SNS retries are limited, so orders for a service offline for hours are lost.

case.label: D
case.text: Messages that are not visible are being processed or are in flight, and a stalled consumer could make that number grow, so a candidate may use it as a signal; it measures messages in flight, not how long messages have waited.
